c.tagline: City of poets, gardens and the Pink Mosque, gateway to ancient Persepolis.

taxi.fareNote: The Snapp and Tapsi apps give fixed fares. Foreign bank cards don't work in Iran, so pay taxis in cash (rials); app wallets are topped up with cash. Agree a fare before boarding shared or street taxis.

emergency.note: Fire: 125. English-speaking operators are not guaranteed; hotel staff can assist.

avoid.reason: Keep valuables close in the crowded Vakil Bazaar and use snap or hotel-arranged taxis rather than hailing unmarked cars at night.

hood_desc: The historic heart of Shiraz built by the Zand dynasty - the Karim Khan Citadel, Vakil Bazaar, Vakil Mosque and traditional teahouses sit within a compact, walkable core; the natural base for first-timers.

The old quarter around the Nasir al-Mulk (Pink) Mosque and the mirror-tiled Shah Cheragh shrine off Lotf Ali Khan Zand Street; a maze of atmospheric lanes and traditional houses, best explored on foot.
A calmer, leafier district on the western side of the city around the UNESCO-listed Eram Garden and Shiraz University; residential and green, quieter than the center.
The area around the tomb of the beloved poet Hafez (Hafezieh) and its gardens, a place of pilgrimage for Iranians; tranquil and cultured, close to the tomb of Saadi to the northeast.
Shiraz's modern, upscale strip along Chamran Boulevard climbing toward the hills, lined with the city's smartest hotels, restaurants and cafes with views over the city.

water.note: Tap water in Shiraz is generally safe to drink, though many visitors stick to cheap bottled water for taste.

transit.pay: Fares are paid with a rechargeable transit smart card tapped at metro gates and on buses; single tickets are available at stations. Foreign bank cards don't work in Iran, so top the card up with cash.
transit.hours: Metro Line 1 runs roughly 06:30-21:30 with buses on a similar schedule; there is no overnight service, so use Snapp or Tapsi late at night.
transit.note: Metro Line 1 crosses the city north-south; the historic Zand core with the bazaar, citadel and Pink Mosque is compact and easily walkable.

train: Shiraz Railway Station - domestic services toward Tehran, Isfahan and Yazd
bus: Karandish (Central) Bus Terminal - intercity coaches across Iran

transit.m: City bus toward the center (30-40 min)
Snapp / Tapsi to the Zand center (15-25 min)

tip.r: Rounding up is appreciated in taxis and restaurants; upscale venues may add a service charge. Not deeply ingrained but increasingly common in tourist-facing places.

food.name: Kalam polo Shirazi
food.desc: Shiraz's signature rice dish: cabbage and tiny herbed meatballs layered through rice scented with tarragon and sweet basil, with a crisp tahdig base.

places.name: Sharzeh Restaurant
places.note: Traditional restaurant beside the Vakil Mosque; live music and the classic Shirazi menu.

places.name: Shapouri Restaurant
places.note: Set in a 1930s Qajar mansion and garden; kalam polo is the dish to order.

places.name: Haft Khan
places.note: Multi-floor complex with a traditional Iranian floor doing regional Fars cooking.

food.name: Haleem bademjan
food.desc: Smoked aubergine pounded with shredded lamb, whey and mint oil into a smoky, creamy dip scooped up with flatbread. Ordered as a starter by everyone.

places.name: Sharzeh Restaurant
places.note: Reliable version in the most atmospheric traditional dining room in town.

places.name: Shater Abbas
places.note: Busy basement restaurant with an open kitchen and a long Persian menu.

places.name: Parhami Traditional House
places.note: Restored mansion with a courtyard pond, fountain and live traditional music.

food.name: Salad Shirazi
food.desc: Finely diced cucumber, tomato and onion dressed with lime juice and dried mint. Named for the city and served alongside almost every meal in Iran.

places.name: Shater Abbas
places.note: Arrives with every kebab order, made fresh and properly sharp.

places.name: Sharzeh Restaurant
places.note: The standard accompaniment to the kebabs and rice dishes.

places.name: Haft Khan
places.note: Good place to try it beside a spread of other Fars specialities.

food.name: Ash-e sabzi Shirazi
food.desc: Thick green soup of herbs, beans and noodles soured with local grape verjuice, topped with fried mint and onion. A Shiraz winter staple.

places.name: Sharzeh Restaurant
places.note: One of the few tourist-friendly places that keeps the regional ash on the menu.

places.name: Parhami Traditional House
places.note: Home-style Shirazi cooking in a small restored courtyard mansion.

places.name: Vakil Bazaar food lanes
places.note: Bazaar kitchens ladle out ash and other soups cheaply at lunchtime.

food.name: Dopiazeh aloo
food.desc: A rough, deeply savoury hash of potato, minced meat, masses of onion and dried plums, eaten with bread. Pure Shirazi home cooking.

places.name: Parhami Traditional House
places.note: Traditional house serving the older Shirazi dishes tourists rarely see.

places.name: Sharzeh Restaurant
places.note: Keeps regional Fars dishes alongside the standard kebabs.

places.name: Vakil Bazaar food lanes
places.note: Small local eateries around the bazaar cook it for weekday lunch.

food.name: Faloodeh Shirazi
food.desc: Frozen threads of rice-starch vermicelli in rose-water and lime syrup, sometimes with a scoop of saffron ice cream. Invented here, eaten year round.

places.name: Faloodeh shops around Shah Cheragh
places.note: Cluster of long-running counters serving faloodeh and masghati by the bowl.

places.name: Vakil Bazaar sweet sellers
places.note: Faloodeh, masghati and Shirazi nougat sold along the bazaar's covered lanes.

places.name: Haft Khan
places.note: Dessert floor does a tidy modern version if you want it sitting down.

food.name: Sharbat-e beedmeshk
food.desc: Musk-willow distillate mixed with iced water, sugar and basil seeds. Shiraz is the centre of Iran's flower-distillate trade. Alcohol is banned nationwide.

places.name: Vakil Bazaar attari (herbalist) shops
places.note: Rows of shops selling rose, willow and orange-blossom distillates by the bottle.

places.name: Saraye Moshir
places.note: Restored two-storey caravanserai courtyard with cafes pouring iced sharbats.

places.name: Parhami Traditional House
places.note: Serves traditional sharbats in the courtyard beside the fountain.

food.name: Persian tea in the gardens
food.desc: Black tea from a samovar with rock sugar or saffron sharbat, drunk under orange trees in Shiraz's garden teahouses. No alcohol is available in Iran.

places.name: Hafezieh teahouse
places.note: Cypress-shaded terrace beside the poet's tomb; the classic Shiraz tea stop.

places.name: Saraye Moshir
places.note: Courtyard cafes in a restored caravanserai, good for tea between bazaar stalls.

places.name: Bagh-e Naranjestan and Eram Garden cafes
places.note: Garden cafes where tea and sweets come with orange-blossom scent in spring.

landmarks: Nasir al-Mulk Mosque (Pink Mosque)
A 19th-century mosque world-famous for morning sunlight streaming through stained-glass windows onto carpets in a kaleidoscope of colour.
Persepolis (Takht-e Jamshid)
The awe-inspiring ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Empire, a UNESCO site of colossal stairways, bull-headed columns and reliefs an hour from Shiraz.
Shah Cheragh Shrine
A dazzling pilgrimage shrine whose domed halls are entirely mirrored in millions of glass shards, glittering like the interior of a diamond.
Eram Garden (Bagh-e Eram)
A UNESCO-listed Persian paradise garden of towering cypresses, roses and a pastel Qajar pavilion reflected in a long turquoise pool.
Tomb of Hafez (Hafezieh)
The marble tomb of Persia's most beloved poet, set beneath a tiled pavilion in a garden where Iranians come to recite his verses at dusk.
Karim Khan Citadel (Arg of Karim Khan)
A massive 18th-century fortress-palace with four round brick towers, one famously leaning, dominating the centre of Shiraz.
Vakil Bazaar
An atmospheric Zand-era covered bazaar of vaulted brick corridors, caravanserais and courtyards piled with carpets, spices and handicrafts.
Vakil Mosque
Karim Khan's magnificent regal mosque, famed for its prayer hall of 48 spiral-carved columns and superbly tiled entrance portal.
Tomb of Saadi (Saadieh)
An elegant columned mausoleum in a garden honouring the 13th-century master poet Saadi, whose verses adorn the tiled interior.
Naqsh-e Rostam
Four monumental royal tombs of Achaemenid kings, including Darius the Great, carved high into a sheer cliff face near Persepolis.

train.note: No international trains. Shiraz has a modern station on a branch line, with overnight services to Tehran taking around 15 hours and trains to Isfahan and Yazd, though the network here is thinner than in central Iran and the bus is usually faster. Raja's booking site is Persian-language and does not take foreign cards - book through a hotel or agent.

bus.note: No international coaches from Shiraz. The Karandish and Amir Kabir terminals run VIP coaches to Isfahan (about 7 hours), Yazd (6), Tehran (12 overnight) and Bandar Abbas; Seiro Safar and Hamsafar are the main operators. Buy at the terminal in cash. Buses to Persepolis are limited - most visitors take a taxi or a tour.

ferry.note: Shiraz is inland in the Zagros mountains with no navigable water, so there are no ferries. The Gulf ferry terminals at Bandar Abbas, for Qeshm and Kish islands, are about 10 hours away by road.

half.name: Pasargadae
half.blurb: The first capital of the Persian Empire, with the simple limestone tomb of Cyrus the Great standing alone on a plain.

half.name: Firuzabad
half.blurb: A Sassanid-era site with the domed ruins of Ardashir's Palace and a hilltop fortress overlooking a fertile valley.

full.name: Bishapur
full.blurb: A Sassanid royal city founded by Shapur I, with a mosaic-floored palace and rock reliefs carved into a nearby gorge.
